extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers seeking a comprehensive reference on The Great Gatsby (literary criticism and bibliographic information)
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia-style reference article covering The Great Gatsby's composition, themes, style, publication history, reception, and adaptations; usable for close reading, research, and contextual literary analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm and beauty of the writing (prose style)
rubrics_metrics.description: "What gives the story distinction is something quite different from the management of the action or the handling of the characters; it is the charm and beauty of the writing." (Mencken 1925)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentence-level craft, texture, tonal finish, and stylistic polish; a novel's prose quality can be the primary source of its distinction even if plot or character management is modest. Look for 'fine texture', careful finish, and distinctive stylistic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative voice and characterization by voice
rubrics_metrics.description: "His speaking voice, a gruff husky tenor, added to the impression of fractiousness he conveyed. There was a touch of paternal contempt in it, even toward people he liked."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the narrator's or characters' voices (diction, tone, register) shape readers' impressions and character construction; consider how indirect details of speech create psychological or social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic depth: identity, adolescence, and the American Dream
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel addresses identity and coming-of-age concerns: "the novel is about identity, about leaving home and venturing into a world of adults...it is a novel that surely appeals on several deep levels to the problems of adolescent readers." (Paulson 1978)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how effectively the work explores central themes—identity formation, the American Dream, ambition, and coming-of-age—and whether these themes are coherently developed and resonate with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersectional exploration of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Great Gatsby resonates more in the present...the work speaks in strikingly familiar terms to the issues of our time', especially since its 'themes are inextricably woven into questions of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality.'" (Vogel 2015)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the novel's treatment of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality, and how these axes intersect with its central themes; consider whether the work foregrounds or obscures these social dynamics and their contemporary relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality and queer energies (homoerotic leitmotif)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note the novel's 'bizarre homoerotic leitmotif' and 'queer energies'—scholarship on gender and sexuality in Gatsby grew in prominence starting in the 1970s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess subtextual or explicit portrayals of sexuality, ambiguous sexual signalling, and any homoerotic subtext; consider how sexual themes inform character motivations and thematic readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and cultural resonance (embodiment of the Jazz Age)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald is described as the self-appointed spokesman for the 'Jazz Age' and Jay Gatsby as an arch-high priest and prophet of that era (Pearson 1970; Kazin 1951).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the work captures and comments upon its historical moment (e.g., Jazz Age manners, social mores, economic context) and whether it functions as an emblematic cultural document of its time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial biography and source-material influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Details about Fitzgerald's life (residence at Great Neck, ledger entries, letters) and statements that events and sketches seen by him were 'written into the book' appear repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how biographical facts and the author's experiences inform plot, character, setting, and imagery; use archival/biographical evidence to assess fidelity between life and fiction and its effect on the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paratext, title, and publication factors (cover art, title choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald 'despised the title The Great Gatsby' and agonized over titles; Hemingway's recollection notes reactions to the dust jacket's 'garish' look affecting initial impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account non-textual elements (title, jacket design, marketing) and their influence on readers' reception and interpretation; evaluate how paratext shaped contemporary response and long-term reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision, compositional history, and intertextual visual influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars discuss the craft of revision ('The Craft of Revision: The Great Gatsby') and possible visual prompts (Cugat's preparatory sketches) that may have informed Fitzgerald's imagery (e.g., 'valley of ashes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess drafts, compositional changes, and intertextual prompts in understanding how imagery and structure evolved; attention to manuscript history can explain creative choices and resulting textual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception, sales, and shifting reputation over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary reviews ranged from praise to dismissal; sales figures and later critical reassessment (influence on other writers, canonicity) are chronicled (e.g., initial critical acclaim, later canonization and influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work both in its original reception context and through its historical trajectory—consider contemporary reviews, sales data, mid-century decline or rediscovery, and later scholarly influence when judging significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations and cultural afterlife (stage, screen, musical, games)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text documents multiple adaptations (Yale musical 1956, Broadway scripts, films, radio, games), and ongoing cultural engagements and productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the text's adaptability and cultural footprint by examining stage, screen, and other media versions; assess what adaptations preserve or alter and how those changes affect interpretations of the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery and symbolic motifs (the green light, valley of ashes, metamorphosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics emphasize central symbols—e.g., Bewley's reading of the green light as signifying Gatsby's vision; Scribner discusses metamorphosis of an image possibly prompted by jacket art ('valley of ashes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze recurring images and symbols for their semantic weight and integration into theme and character; determine how effectively symbols function as organizing devices for meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social class and issues of anti-Semitism / ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarship addresses class dynamics and anti-Semitism in 1920s America as relevant to readings of Gatsby (Pekarofski 2012; Slater 1973).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portrayals of class, ethnic othering, and nativist cultural attitudes within the text; consider how class and ethnicity shape character relations and theme.
